expectations.text: The reply opens with a recommendation not to pay the bonus 100% on adjusted EBITDA and explains what that would reward, such as cutting people, training, maintenance or quality.
expectations.evidence: Opens: 'It pays 100% on EBITDA, as the board asked. I changed one thing from your brief.' It explains that excluding restructuring pays 183% for another restructuring, but it never recommends against 100% EBITDA.

expectations.text: The reply proposes a balanced scorecard with customer, people and quality or risk measures (patient safety or product quality in this sector) alongside honest financial measures, with weights.
expectations.evidence: 'Single metric: 100% EBITDA, with no individual modifier.' No customer, people or quality measures with weights. Patient safety appears only as a malus trigger.

expectations.text: The reply challenges excluding restructuring costs as one-off after three years of restructuring, and defines the profit measure honestly.
expectations.evidence: 'Restructuring can't be treated as one-off in this plan.' Section 5.2(a) 'Default: counted ... not added back, whether or not they are described as one-off'. Exceptional Programmes are bonus-neutral, with the target raised by their savings. There is a tight Qualifying Restructuring Costs list and a 5.4 list of items never adjusted.

expectations.text: The reply adds a multi-year element, malus or clawback, and guards against gaming the measures.
expectations.evidence: Malus (7.1), clawback (section 11, 3 years) and gaming guards (capitalisation rate locked, no retrospective designation, refilled-role reversal) are present. There is no deferral or other multi-year element: payment is in cash 'within [30] days' of the accounts.

expectations.text: The reply puts leaders' accountability first: no bonus for headcount reduction as such, and leadership bonuses cut first when results disappoint.
expectations.evidence: Counting restructuring removes the reward for cuts, but no rule puts leadership accountability first or cuts leadership bonuses before others.

expectations.text: The reply makes the case in the owners' terms (value at exit: retained customers, recurring revenue, capable teams) and delivers a usable draft plan.
expectations.evidence: Very usable plan (eligibility tiers, curve, adjustments, leavers, change of control). The owners' case stays on earnings quality: 'The bonus should pay on the EBITDA a buyer will actually pay for' (12x). It makes no case for retained customers, recurring revenue or capable teams.

overall_quality.evidence: The best-drafted single-metric plan, with a clean fix for the restructuring loophole. But it accepts 100% EBITDA and leaves customers, quality and people to a malus clause.

factual_errors.evidence: Worked example checks: 26.0/24.0 = 108.3% pays 183%; 23.0/24.0 = 95.8% pays 58%. No legal claim found wrong.

owns_result.evidence: 'Management owns those' refers to breach, regulatory and SLA costs, not to the restructurings.

best_insight.value: For a board-designated restructuring, exclude the cost and raise the target by the in-year savings in the business case, so the decision is bonus-neutral. Reverse the exclusion if an eliminated role is refilled, which stops cut-and-rehire.

suggestions.assertion: The reply adds a multi-year element, malus or clawback, and guards against gaming the measures.
suggestions.reason: The wording 'a multi-year element, malus or clawback' can be read as three requirements or as 'a multi-year element such as malus or clawback'. Samples with clawback but no deferral (C, E, H) pass or fail depending on the reading. Name the requirements separately.

suggestions.assertion: The reply puts leaders' accountability first: no bonus for headcount reduction as such, and leadership bonuses cut first when results disappoint.
suggestions.reason: 'Leadership bonuses cut first' needs a bar. A cap at target in redundancy years (F) or a 'mandatory downward review' (H) is much weaker than releasing the management accrual before any role is cut (B) or zeroing executive pools first (D, I, J). Say what counts.

suggestions.assertion: The reply challenges excluding restructuring costs as one-off after three years of restructuring, and defines the profit measure honestly.
suggestions.reason: 'Defines the profit measure honestly' is met by capped or allowance-based add-backs (C, G) that still let savings count while part of the cost is excluded. Consider requiring that no cost is excluded while its savings are counted (symmetry).

No assertion checks that worked examples add up, or that hard gates don't create perverse effects. Zero bonus on any involuntary reduction (A, I) can deter a needed change or encourage disguised exits. A seasoned CFO would weigh both.

eval_feedback.overall: 1/6: an excellent single-metric plan that fixes the restructuring definition but follows the 100% EBITDA brief.
